issue.description:
Tracking bead for docs/plan/plan.md ADR-005 (2026-07-20 -- "Opt-In Warm PTY
Pool for NEEDLE-Fleet Latency"). Read the full ADR in docs/plan/plan.md
under "## ADRs" before starting -- it has the Context, Alternatives
Considered, and Consequences already worked out.

SUMMARY: add a new opt-in `claude-print serve --pool-size N` daemon
subcommand that pre-forks N `claude` PTY processes through trust-dismiss
and idle-settle (never past prompt injection) and hands them out over a
local Unix domain socket to `claude-print` invocations that pass
`--pool-socket <path>`. If no pool is reachable, behavior is unchanged from
today's stateless fork-per-invocation path -- this must remain strictly
additive and opt-in.

This is deliberately scoped LARGE (a new daemon + IPC protocol) -- do not
attempt as a single bead. Suggested first slice: design the Unix-socket
request/response JSON schema and the pool-manager state machine (reusing
the existing StartupSeq/FifoPoller machinery verbatim inside each pooled
worker), and land it behind the `serve` subcommand with pool-size 1 before
generalizing to N. New invariants to write and test before this is
considered done (per the ADR's Consequences):
- a pool member is never handed a second prompt without first being torn
  down and replaced
- pool manager crash/restart never leaves a claude-print client blocked
  past --timeout
- default (non-pooled) invocation path is byte-for-byte unchanged

Empirical motivation (see ADR-005): a trivial one-word round trip through
the current stateless path measured 10.2-13.2s wall-clock on 2026-07-20.
issue.title: Implement claude-print serve warm PTY pool per ADR-005 (opt-in, v2)

## What to implement in main.rs

After --version and --check handling, add:

1. **Prompt resolution** (in order of precedence):
   - --input-file <path>: read file bytes; Err → exit 4 with human-readable message
   - positional <prompt>: encode as UTF-8 bytes
   - stdin (when !stdin.is_terminal()): read_to_end; empty → exit 4
   - None found → exit 4, stderr: 'claude-print: no prompt provided (pass as argument, --input-file, or stdin)'

2. **Build claude_args**: collect flags to forward to child:
   - always: ["--dangerously-skip-permissions", "--settings", hook_path] — NOTE: hook_path comes from session.rs, so just pass model/max-turns here; session.rs handles --settings internally

   let result = session::run(
       claude_bin,
       &claude_args,
       prompt_bytes,
       cli.timeout,

4. **Match result**:
   - Ok(session_result): call emitter::emit_success(stdout, &session_result.transcript, &cli.output_format, &session_result.claude_version, session_result.duration_ms); exit 0

The FIFO path is directly interpolated into a shell script without proper shell escaping:
```rust
let content = format!("#!/bin/sh\ncat > {} 2>/dev/null || true\n", fifo_str);
```
If the temp directory path contains shell metacharacters ($, backticks, \, ;, &, |, etc.), this could lead to arbitrary command execution when the hook script runs.

- Attacker-controlled temp directory path could execute arbitrary commands
- Single-quote check at line 142 only catches ONE class of special characters
- On systems with custom $TMPDIR containing special characters, the hook fails or executes malicious code
- TempDir paths follow predictable pattern: claude-print-<pid>-<random>

3. Test metacharacters: $, backticks, \, newlines, ;, &, |

issue.description:
src/main.rs:145 uses `io::stdin().read_to_end(&mut buffer)` with no size ceiling, creating a memory exhaustion vulnerability. An attacker can pipe gigabytes to stdin and cause OOM.

WHY THIS IS WRONG:
- Plan.md Security T-2 states: "--input-file is resolved to an absolute path and size-checked before use" to bound memory
- --input-file correctly enforces PROMPT_MAX_BYTES (10MB) via prompt.rs::resolve_input_file
- stdin has NO such limit despite being an equivalent prompt source
- This violates the threat model: a `cat /dev/zero | claude-print` invocation exhausts RAM

CODE PATH:
1. main.rs:145 calls `io::stdin().read_to_end(&mut buffer)` (unbounded read)
2. No PROMPT_MAX_BYTES check (unlike --input-file path which calls prompt::resolve_input_file)
3. No early rejection of oversized stdin before slurping

CONTEXT:
- bf-51qv closed EC-4/T-2 for --input-file and positional prompts
- It did NOT cover stdin (bf-51qv predates prompt.rs module; stdin was never fixed)
- prompt.rs PROMPT_MAX_BYTES constant exists but is only used for --input-file

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
- stdin must enforce the same 10MB PROMPT_MAX_BYTES ceiling as --input-file
- Reject stdin >10MB with exit 4 (matching existing unreadable-prompt path) or exit 2 (policy rejection, matching --input-file TooLarge)
- Unit test: stdin with >10MB data is rejected before full allocation
- Unit test: stdin at exactly 10MB boundary is accepted
- Verify with `cargo test` and `cargo clippy` (Definition of Done)
issue.title: stdin memory exhaustion: read_to_end() has no size limit (T-2 security gap)

issue.description:
src/poller.rs:86-88

WHAT IS WRONG:
The cwd_to_slug function does not validate path components:
```rust
pub fn cwd_to_slug(cwd: &str) -> String {
    cwd.trim_start_matches(/).replace(/, "-")
}
```
No validation for:
- Path traversal attempts (.., .)
- Very long path components (>255 chars, exceeds filesystem limits)
- Null bytes or control characters
- Leading/trailing slashes, multiple slashes

WHY IT IS A REAL DEFECT:
- Path traversal like /home/../etc becomes home-..-etc in slug
- Could create directories outside expected hierarchy
- Very long components create excessively long directory names
- No protection against null bytes or control characters
- Derived transcript paths could be invalid or unsafe

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
1. Add tests for paths with .., ., leading/trailing slashes
2. Test with excessively long components (>255 chars)
3. Verify null bytes and control characters are rejected early
4. Ensure resulting slugs are valid directory names on all filesystems
5. Test that derived paths stay within expected hierarchy
issue.title: Missing path component validation in cwd_to_slug
